street_king.title: Street King
epilogue: A year later. You sit in the plastic chair at the motor park office. It still has Baba Ticket's shape in it.

epilogue.text: Baba Ticket now sells suya two streets away. He gives you extra pepper. You are never sure it is a kindness.
Baba Ticket retired to his third wife's house in Ìkòròdú. He calls every Friday to quote a proverb wrong.

epilogue: Every morning the drivers line up and pay. Some pay because they respect you. Some pay because they remember Scatter's glasses in the puddle.

epilogue.text: The co-op board still stands beside Ada's Corner. Three o's. You never let anybody fix it.

epilogue: At 5:40 a.m. a boy steps off the night bus with a phone on 3% battery. Somebody who is definitely not a conductor walks towards him.
You stand up. "Oya. Come here, JJC."
street_king.hint: Earn Baba Ticket's chair, or take it.

cult_boss.title: Cult Boss
epilogue: The curtain at the Shell House opens for the first time in twenty years.
Behind it: a desk, a stamp, a very old man in a brown cardigan, and nine thousand files.
"Number One Shell," he says, and slides the stamp across the desk. "You cannot refuse. Nobody ever could. That is why nobody asks."

epilogue.text: Ada does not come to the ceremony. She sends a note: "Ask for the receipt."
Somewhere in the files there is one with Sunday's name on it. You never open it. You never throw it away either.

epilogue: You sit. The chair is warm. Outside, the Hyenas are quiet, and the junction pays its dues on time.
Your first official act is to sign Form T-12 for a nervous boy with a phone on 3% battery. Nine pages. In triplicate.
cult_boss.hint: Rise through the Shell and win the war.

wanted.title: Wanted
epilogue: Night. The back of Formula One's okada. No helmet, no plan, one bag.
"Where we dey go?" he shouts over the engine.
"Anywhere wey road go."
Behind you, Iyana-Wahala's lights shrink to one orange dot under the flyover. A green van sits at the junction with its siren off.

epilogue.text: Bassey is in the van. He watches you go. He does not radio anybody. Not tonight.
Your phone buzzes. Iya Bọ́sẹ̀. You let it ring all the way to Ogun State.

epilogue: Formula One laughs into the wind. For the first time since you arrived, so do you.
wanted.hint: Let the police heat run hot, and make the wrong enemies.

legit_businessman.title: Legit Businessman

epilogue.text: Iyana-Wahala Transport Ltd. Three yellow danfos. A real office with a real receipt book.
Iyana-Wahala Transport Ltd, owned by the Okafor family. Three yellow danfos. Ada does the accounts. Nobody argues with the accounts.
Ada is your business partner. Her first rule: no fee without receipt. Her second rule: no receipt without fee.

epilogue: The first danfo is called "Rule Number One". Bíọ́dún drives it, singing.

epilogue.text: Sunday is the conductor. He dances at every stop. Passengers tip him to stop dancing. He takes the money and dances more.

epilogue: Your drivers pay one fair fee to one co-operative and nobody else.
Some mornings you still wake up at 5:40, ready to run.
legit_businessman.hint: Save your hustle money and stay clear of the cults.

informant.title: The Informant
epilogue: Abuja. A two-bedroom flat with air conditioning, a guard, and nothing to do.
Your new name is Emmanuel. You keep forgetting it.

epilogue.text: On TV, Barrister Settlement leaves a courthouse with his face covered by a very expensive file folder.
On TV, the Shell House is sealed with yellow tape. Somebody has stamped the tape. Twice.

epilogue: The food here is fine. It is just... fine. You would sell your new name for one plate of Mama Put's ewa agoyin.
At night you call out bus stops in your sleep. The guard has started answering.
informant.hint: Give Commander Bassey what he wants.

rock_bottom.title: Rock Bottom

epilogue.text: You wake up in a ward at General Hospital Iyana-Wahala. Nurse Rónkẹ́ is counting drips like money.
The election ends. The posters peel. You are standing at the Back Side with nothing: no crew, no co-op, no shell, no savings.

epilogue: "You again," says Nurse Rónkẹ́, and then, softer: "Eat something."
Your phone rings. It's Mama. You don't have the strength to lie any more.
"{name}, come home. We go find the money together. Market women no dey kill person. Dem just dey talk until you wish dem kill you."
You laugh. It hurts. You laugh anyway.

jailed.title: Jailed
epilogue: Awaiting Trial. Cell 4. Forty men, one window, one bucket.

epilogue.text: A man in the corner holds up a hand with three fingers. "Ah," says Professor. "Rule number thirteen: never get caught. I forgot to teach you that one."
An old man in the corner squints at you. "Iyana-Wahala? Jimoh Professor's boy? Sit down. I was his cellmate in '98. Let me teach you the rules of the cell."
Every Sunday, Ada brings moi-moi and the accounts. Every Sunday she says, "Next month."

epilogue: Your case file is on a desk somewhere, under nine other case files.
Outside, somebody else is calling your stop.
jailed.hint: Be the hottest name on the street when the Sweep comes.

go_home.title: Go Home
epilogue: The last alert goes through at 9:14 a.m. ₦0 owing.
In Ìlú-Àlàáfíà, Iya Bọ́sẹ̀ reads the message twice, puts down her phone, and declares a market holiday nobody asked for.
You go home in Bíọ́dún's danfo. "God's Time Is The Best" is full of gifts: rice, a generator, a framed photo of the Iyana-Wahala co-op board, three o's.
Mama is standing at the junction when you arrive. She looks at you for a long time. Then she slaps your arm, hard, and doesn't let go of it.

epilogue.text: Ada comes too. Mama inspects her like a goat at market, then gives her the best chair.
Professor sends a voice note: "Rule number one hundred: go home while home is still there. Well done, my son."

epilogue: That night the whole town eats. Nobody mentions Double-Double. Everybody mentions it the next morning.
go_home.hint: Pay every naira. Keep your hands and your friendships clean.

the_honourable.title: The Honourable
epilogue: Councillor {name}, Iyana-Wahala Ward. Independent. Elected by a margin nobody could rig because everybody was watching.
Hon. Mrs. Ronke Ademola-Peters sends flowers. Hon. Owó Ńlá sends a lawyer. Barrister Settlement sends his congratulations, and his card, in case.
Your first act in office is a community feeding programme.
The rice bags arrive on Monday. Your face is printed on every one of them.
You stare at the bags for a long time.
Then you sign for them.
The cycle continues.
the_honourable.hint: Expose the right man, in front of the right crowd.

_fates.text: Professor: buried under the flyover's shadow. On his grave someone painted Rule Number One.
Professor: serving the time that should have been yours. He runs the prison canteen. Badly.
Professor: Professor's Kitchen, beside Mama Put. The rules are on the wall. Rule number one is still spelled wrong.
Professor: teaching goats the rules of the road in his sister's village.
Professor: same corner, same chair, watching the Back Side.
Ada: together with you, when you're honest. Saving for university. Still laughing at your lies.
Ada: your best friend. Her shop has a second container now.
Ada: she got into university. She didn't tell you. You heard from Mallam Garba.
Sunday: out of the Hyenas. Still dancing at every stop.
Sunday: still a Hyena on paper. Still your friend in secret.
Sunday: gone. Some nights you hear a conductor laugh and you turn around.
Scatter: runs Under-Bridge "with your permission". He is still 5'4". He still asks you not to mention it.
Scatter: still waiting for his turn. Lagos is round.
Mama's debt: paid in full. Iya Bọ́sẹ̀ has found someone new to send voice notes to.
Mama's debt: {debt} still owing. The voice notes continue.
Ada: you said sorry properly, once. She still brings it up when she's winning an argument.
Ada: knows every naira of Mama's debt. She helped pay the last ₦20,000 and pretends she didn't.
Mama: still has your first voice note from Lagos. "I reach, Mama." She plays it when NEPA takes the light.
Commander Bassey: still remembers the boy who said nothing in his cell. "Quiet ones," he says, "na dem I watch."
Commander Bassey: still raids every rainy season. He greets you by name. That's not a good sign.
Your first ₦2,000 to the Task Force is still in a file somewhere. Bassey keeps everything.
Bassey: refused your money, twice. He's the only officer on the junction you can't buy. You respect him for it, a little.
Professor: still tells people how you begged to meet Baba Ticket on day one. "Eager like goat for yam."
Professor: still remembers you asked about his cut on your first day. "That boy go far," he says. He isn't sure it's a compliment.
Kúnlé: Professor's son, the one called Giggles. You never told anyone whose laugh it was.
Kpakpa: still tells people Professor saved you. Professor doesn't correct him.
Kpakpa: you beat him on your first week. He sells phone chargers now, and avoids your eyes.
Kpakpa: beat you on your first week. He's mentioned it every day since.
Baba Ticket: still tells new boys how you accepted ₦15,000 quota without blinking. "Fool or lion. We never know."
Baba Ticket's ledger: there's still one line from your first night. "₦0 — tomorrow."
Your first fee was ₦500, like everybody's. You stopped being like everybody later.
The drivers at Front Stop: they still remember the boy who explained the fuel hike instead of hiding it.
Bíọ́dún: still laughs about the day you chased him for ₦500. He paid in the end. Mostly in jokes.
Bíọ́dún's danfo: still missing a conductor every Tuesday.
Bíọ́dún's danfo: still has your slogan painted on the back. The paint is peeling. The slogan isn't.
Your first Red-Eye Tonic: still the worst ₦600 you ever spent. Your eyes remember.
Scatter: never forgot your first day. He is short. His memory is long.
Scatter: beat you under the bridge once. He has a photo. He shows it to people.
Scatter's boys: still say you were "one of us" at the rally. You weren't. Nobody believes you.
Under-Bridge: you said you'd think about it when you got there. You did. Too late, but you did.
The rally: you got beaten for ₦15,000. The candidate never learned your name.
Settlement: still has your number under "Rally — cheap".
Settlement: still tells people you're the only boy who ever bargained with him. He raised his prices after you.
Chuks: still remembers you followed him into the Shell without asking where you were going.
Chuks's first lesson: some people you must not beg. Ever. You still remember the list.
Zone 5: the beggars there still chase you away. You were bad at it. They were proud of you anyway.
The Big Man's nephew: still angry. He has a lot of free time and a long memory.
You stood on your own two legs. Some days they shook. They held.
The Shell: you chose them at the crossroads. They chose you back, with conditions.
Number One Shell: you asked who he was, once. He still doesn't know your name. That's what saves you.
The Shell's initiation: you remember every answer. You'd rather not.
The convoy: Owó Ńlá's outriders still have your face on a phone somewhere.
The convoy: you stood aside for Owó Ńlá's sirens once. He waved. You didn't wave back.
The ward levy: you paid it every time. Nobody knows where it went. Everybody knows.
The little girl you walked round the market: her mother sells you oranges for half price. Forever.
Nurse Rónkẹ́: still remembers the area boy who carried a sick child to her clinic. She gives you plasters for free.
The two conductors you pulled apart: they're best friends now. They fight with each other's enemies.
The hospital: still has your bill. And your name. And a photo.
The hospital window you climbed out of: they fitted bars. Your doing.
Kelvin: paid back his debts, ₦500 at a time. He waves at you every morning.
Kelvin: ran. Nobody knows where. His creditors ask you.
Brother Taiwo: still "healed" every Sunday at the crusade. You helped with the first miracle.
The crusade: the prophet moved to another state after you exposed him. Same miracle, new crowd.
Iya Keke: still pays you back for the stolen keke, ₦200 at a time, with interest she invented.
Formula One: still owes you for the impound run. He pays in free rides.
The co-op board: one fair fee, still written in chalk. Drivers touch it for luck.
Mama's eyes: twenty-twenty in the left, "good enough to see you lying" in the right.
Dr. Okonjo at the general hospital: still owes Professor a story nobody wants told. He fixes eyes for free on the first Monday of every month "for the old man".
Baba Ticket's notebook: one line, in red, from the week your mother came. "45,000. Paid late. Forgiven. Not forgotten."
The impound yard dog: still chases every yellow danfo that passes, just in case.
Professor's rule book: in your back pocket, soft as cloth now.
Professor's rule book: you left it on his chair. Garba keeps it behind his kettle, waiting for the next one who argues.
The JJC from the night bus: he never paid the loading fee. He tells the story the way you would.

grace_grace.title: Grass to Grace
epilogue: A year later. A spare-parts shop in Nkwọ-Agụụ junction, the first one between here and the city. Honest parts. The sign says EMEKA & SONS, though there are no sons yet.

epilogue.text: There are no sons yet. Chinwe says to be patient. Chinwe says a lot of things. You listen to all of them.
On market days, Ọnyịsị buys his bicycle chain from you and tells the story of the thief who confessed under the tree. He improves it every time.
Nne sits outside the shop in the afternoons and tells customers what you did in Lagos. All of it. She is proud of the coming back, not the going.

epilogue: It is not much money. It is yours.
Grace, it turns out, is not the opposite of grass. It's what grows on it when you stop burning the field.
grace_grace.hint: Come home with a clean conscience and no debts.

grace_unbound.title: Unbound
epilogue: The page burns blue, then white, then nothing. Thirty miles away in Zone 5, a white book closes by itself.
Chief Ọ̀dụ̀ stands very still in the firelight. For the first time anybody can remember, he looks old.

epilogue.text: Papa's name rises out of the fire as smoke. The old men say they saw his face in it. The old men say a lot of things on festival nights.
The next morning Nne calls you from the kitchen. By your name. Twice. Just to hear it.
Chinwe looks at you at the festival and frowns, as if remembering a dream. A week later she knocks on your door. 'I think I know you,' she says. 'Tell me how.'

epilogue: The money goes with the page. All of it. The Benz won't start. The house in Zone 5 belongs to someone else's cousin now.
You are poor, and free, and the drums are very loud.
grace_unbound.hint: Find out how the book's hold is broken.

grace_witness.title: The Witness
epilogue: Federal High Court, Lagos. Day forty of the trial. You are in the witness box for the ninth time.
Chief Ọ̀dụ̀ sits in the dock in a grey suit. He looks smaller without the white.

epilogue.text: You go to prison too: eighteen months, reduced for cooperation. Commander Bassey visits on Sundays and brings akara. He says it's for the case. It's not for the case.
You walk out of court each evening a free man with a police escort and a very long memory.

epilogue: The white book is Exhibit 14. It sits in a glass case. Nobody in the courtroom will look at it for long.

epilogue.text: Ike testifies by video from a country with good weather. At the end, for the first time in years, he laughs. The judge has to call for order.

grace_witness.hint: Tell the truth to the one man who has been following the Chief.

grace_goldenCage.title: Golden Cage
epilogue: Zone 5. A gate that opens by itself. A garden with lights in the trees. A house too big to have a sound in it.
You have everything. You count it every night. It doesn't like to be counted. You count it anyway.

epilogue.text: Nne calls on Sundays. She says 'my son' and 'my child' and 'you'. She never says your name. You never ask her to.
You have covered every mirror in the house with white cloth. It seemed like the right colour.
Sometimes you think you see Ike at the gate. It's always the gardener.

epilogue: Outside, Lagos laughs at something. The sound doesn't reach the house.

grace_whiteCloth.title: The White Cloth
epilogue: The cloth is soft. Softer than anything you have ever worn. It fits as if it was cut for you years ago.
You ride back to Lagos in the third white car. Behind you, the festival fire gets smaller, then it's a star, then it's gone.
A year later you sit in the white room. A boy from a village you've never heard of sits in the white chair. His eyes are hungry.
You ask him who he loves most in the world.
You don't laugh. You can't remember when you stopped.
grace_whiteCloth.hint: Let the fellowship keep its hold on you.

grace_prodigal.title: The Prodigal
epilogue: You stay. You have nothing. You have the morning.

epilogue.text: Nne makes you pepper soup and doesn't ask any questions. She doesn't need to. She watches you eat like you are still nine years old.
Nne lets you sleep in the parlour. She is polite to you, which is the worst thing a mother can be.
You owe the village {villageDebt}. You go back to the quarry. Every stone is a naira. It will take years. You start anyway.
At Chinwe's wedding you dance at the back, badly, and nobody minds.

epilogue: On the third morning, Dibia Ọ̀kwụ̀ walks past your door and nods. Not approval. Recognition. That's enough to start with.
grace_prodigal.hint: Come home with nothing but yourself.

_fates_grace.text: Papa's land: still the family's. Yams grow there. Papa would have complained about how they're planted.
Papa's land: fenced, sold, someone else's. Nne walks the long way round it to the stream.
The school roof: finished. The children don't know whose money it was. That's how it should be.
The school roof: still leaking. When it rains, the children move their benches and keep reading.
Ike: far away, still running, almost laughing.
Ike: nobody knows. You know. You don't say.
Ike: taken by the white cars. His mother still sets a plate for him on Sundays.
Chinwe: your wife. She keeps the accounts and your secrets, in that order.
Chinwe: she chose you, in front of her whole family. Her father hasn't forgiven either of you. He's coming round.
The driver with the failed brakes: he still tells passengers about the JJC who sold him fake parts. He doesn't know your name. He describes your face very accurately.
The driver with the failed brakes: you paid for his repairs. He brings you his customers now.
The village: it believed you about Ike, mostly. Some of the elders still look at you a second too long.
The white book: you never read it. Some nights you wonder what your page said.
Nne: she still says 'ask yourself if you'll tell me at Christmas'. You still do.
The gate in Zone 5: you never went near it again. You still run, in dreams.
Commander Bassey: he kept your file. He keeps everybody's file. Yours has a note in the margin: 'village boy. watch.'
The money: you gave some of it away. It's the only part you remember spending.
Dibia Ọ̀kwụ̀: still peeling oranges by the stream. Still right about most things.
Nne: you told her everything was fine. She let you believe she believed it.
The white envelope: you burned it. Some nights you still smell gold ink.
The white chair: you ran from it. It is still waiting, they say, in a house with no number.
The fleet manager with the duck tie: he buys only from Mama Ngozi now. His buses have the best brakes on Ikorodu Road.
You swore on Papa's grave that fake brake pads were original. Papa's grave has not said anything. Yet.
The beggars under the bridge: they still talk about the man who gave away white-thread money in handfuls, like it was burning him.
Papa Ngwo's burial: they still say Nwankwo's son gave ₦50,000. Each year the number grows. Last year it was ₦200,000.
Kalu: he turned up at the dibia's shrine one rainy night, in white, shaking. The old man let him in.
Kalu: an usher now, with soft gloves and a soft voice. He never laughs.
Kalu: still at Ngozi's stall, still in love with every Benz, still running from white Lexuses. He laughs like a market.
Nne's good wrapper from Lagos: she wears it only to church, and only when the pastor is preaching about prodigal sons.
The compound still talks about the Peak milk.
Ike's mother: she knows about the white cars now. She goes to the stream every evening and calls his name, in case it helps.
Uncle Dozie: "Dozie and Associates" has opened in Onitsha. Same business card. Different victims.
Uncle Dozie: home, quieter, and very good at peeling yams at funerals.

u_firstClass.title: First Class, Fair and Square
epilogue: Your name is read out with the words 'First Class Honours'. Mama screams so loudly that the VC stops and smiles.

epilogue.text: Everybody knows whose son you are now. Her pap stand outside the gate has a queue of graduates.
Half the students you tutored come to shake your hand. One of them cries.

epilogue: You did it without one bought mark. Royal Crest offers you a graduate assistant job. You take it, and you're strict about handouts.
u_firstClass.hint: Ace your exams without buying a single mark.

u_graduate.title: Somtochukwu, Son of the Pap Seller
epilogue: You walk across the stage. Mama is standing on a chair at the back, waving a pap ladle.

epilogue.text: Tamara sits next to her. They've already argued about how much sugar goes in pap. Mama won.
On Monday you start at Hon. Ronke's office. She introduces you as 'the boy who told me the truth'.
The cafeteria still sells your akara. They put your name on it. It's spelled wrong.

epilogue: It isn't a first class. It's a degree with your real name on it, and the right woman in the crowd.
u_graduate.hint: Let Mama stand beside you where everyone can see.

u_goldenLie.title: The Golden Lie
epilogue: You walk the stage as Somto of Bonny Deep Energy. The Ademola-Peters family claps politely.

epilogue.text: Tamara stopped asking questions. That's either love or tiredness. You don't ask which.
Mama watched from a quiet corner. You told her it was for her own good. She nodded. She always nods.
Mama went home on the first danfo. She didn't wait for the photos.

epilogue: Five years later you have a house in Lekki, a job you hate and a story you can never stop telling.

u_viral.title: The Story
epilogue: The campus paper's headline is picked up by every newspaper in Lagos: 'SORTING RACKET AT ROYAL CREST'. Your name is next to Ife's.

epilogue.text: Dr. Fasanya's sacking letter is framed in the student union office.
You collect your certificate a week later, in an office, with no crowd. You don't mind.

epilogue: Three universities set up sexual-harassment panels that summer. A journalism school offers you a place. Ife takes the other one.
u_viral.hint: Help Ife, keep the evidence, and put your name on it.

u_donsCapo.title: Capo
epilogue: Convocation goes on without you. You're at the back gate, in red, giving orders.

epilogue.text: Spike carries your bag now. He hates it. He does it.

epilogue: The money is good. The nights are long. Every new student who reaches the gate reminds you of yourself in first year. You stop looking at their faces.
u_donsCapo.hint: Say yes to the Dons, every time.

u_bigMansBoy.title: The Honourable's Boy
epilogue: Owó Ńlá's car is air-conditioned and smells of new leather. Your new job: 'special assistant on youth matters'.

epilogue.text: The scholarship he gave you was never free. Now you know the price: everything you'll ever say.

epilogue: Tamara's mother loses the election by four thousand votes. You know which four thousand. You were there.
u_bigMansBoy.hint: Take the politician's money and do what he asks.

u_dubai.title: Cotonou
epilogue: The night bus crosses the border at 4 a.m. You have five million naira and a SIM card in someone else's name.

epilogue.text: The Task Force has your photo. Dubai is somewhere in Ghana. He doesn't answer your calls.

epilogue: You send Mama money every month through three different agents. She never asks where it comes from. She never spends it.
u_dubai.hint: Take Dubai's last job, and outrun what follows.

u_expelled.title: Expelled
epilogue: You leave Royal Crest the way you came: through the main gate, with one bag.

epilogue.text: The leaked paper cost you four years. It was worth ₦20,000.

epilogue: Mama meets you at the bus stop. She doesn't ask. She hands you a cup of pap and a tray of akara. 'Help me sell,' she says. You do.
u_expelled.hint: Get caught where the panel can see.

u_cell.title: Remand
epilogue: Eleven months awaiting trial. Your lawyer is a law student from Royal Crest working for free. She's quite good.

epilogue.text: Tobi visits every month. He brings suya and the latest campus gossip. He never mentions Bonny Deep Energy.

epilogue: When you finally walk out, the danfo to Iyana-Wahala costs ₦300 more than it used to. Everything does.
u_cell.hint: Take Dubai's job, and don't run fast enough.

u_home.title: Back to the Bus Stop
epilogue: The danfo to Iyana-Wahala is full. You sit on the edge of a bench with your gown in a nylon bag.

epilogue.text: No certificate until the fees are paid. Four years, waiting in a bursar's drawer.
Tamara sent one message: 'Good luck, whoever you are.' You read it until the bus stop.

epilogue: Mama's stand is where it always was. The degree, or the lack of it, doesn't change the price of pap. You pick up a ladle.
u_home.hint: Leave with what you came with.

_fates_campus.text: Mama: told the whole convocation crowd about her son. Twice.
Mama: went home alone. She keeps your matriculation photo face-down.
Mama: proud, from a corner, as usual.
Tamara: learned to make pap. Badly. Mama approves anyway.
Your school fees: paid by Tamara. You're paying her back, ₦20,000 a month. She frames every receipt.
Hon. Ronke: won her seat. She says a student warned her family once. She never says who.
Tamara: blocked your number. Her mother's lawyers have your name.
Tamara: still waiting for you to tell her the truth.
Ife: now a reporter. Her first front page had your name on it.
Ife: published anyway. Your name isn't in it. You're not sure if you're relieved.
Spike: still at the back gate, still looking for the boy who named him.
The Crimson Dons: still recruiting. The file you gave the VC is still 'missing'.
Dubai: arrested in Ghana six months later. He told the police you were 'the only honest boy at Royal Crest'.
Dr. Fasanya: sacked. He teaches 'business ethics' online now.
'Somto's Akara': still sold at the cafeteria. Still badly.
Final CGPA: {stat:cgpa}. Good enough for anything you want to try.
Final CGPA: {stat:cgpa}. Some employers will ask. Most won't care.
The Foundation photograph: Mama with her ladle in front of the Honourable's banner. It ended up on the Foundation's website by mistake. It's still the best picture they have.
You promised Mama the truth "every time" on your last night at home. She kept count.
Debate Society: they still play the recording of your first-year debate to scare freshers.
Chapel Choir: they sang at your convocation without being asked. Off-key. Perfect.
QuickCash: Mama paid it back with you, ₦2,000 a week, with a notebook. She still has the notebook.
QuickCash: Mama found the messages on your phone in final year. She didn't say anything. She just stopped answering unknown numbers.
Garba's tea: famous now. "As mentioned by a Royal Crest scholar at the Honourable's event." He put it on a signboard.
The green T-shirt from Owó Ńlá's rally: you use it to clean your shoes.
Samuelson chapter nine: you can still recite it. Nobody has ever asked.
Ronke's town hall: scattered by red bandanas. She never found out you were one of them. Tamara did.
Tobi: he still calls you "Campaign Manager" in group chats. He means it as a title.
Tobi's union fixed the hostel water. Nobody has ever thanked him for anything more sincerely.
Ronke's market sanitation brief: three new toilets. Traders call them "the scholar's toilets". You have never been so proud of a toilet.
PayWahala: Mr. Effiong still has your akara spreadsheet on the wall. Next to it, a job offer with your name on it.
The sewing machines: still being photographed, still going back into the warehouse. You know exactly how many.
QuickCash: shut down after the Wahala FM story. Somewhere, a thousand mothers stopped getting phone calls.
The Honourable's favour: he saved Mama's stall and bulldozed Garba's table. He reminds you every election.
The petition: two hundred thumbprints, framed in Ada's new shop.
Mama's corner: rubble, then a filling station. She sells from a cooler at the motor park now. The drivers found her in a day.
Your final-year project: bought at the back gate. Its title was about "cement prices in Abuja". You never read it.
The Akara Index: Dr. Adébáyọ̀ submitted it to a journal. It was accepted. Mama's prices are now cited in footnotes.
Tamara at Iyana-Wahala: nine akara, a burnt tongue and an argument with Garba. The street approves.
You told Tamara your mother was "travelling". Mama has never left Lagos State.
On your last night at home you told Mama: the truth for her, "whatever keeps me there" for everyone else. She has been watching which was which ever since.

p_peoples.title: The People's Honourable
epilogue: The swearing-in is in the community hall. The generator works for the first time in a year.
Six months later, the market has two toilets and a padlock with a key everybody has.

epilogue.text: Mama Titi keeps the notebook. Every quarter she reads it out at the market, and ticks things off with a red biro, in front of everybody.

p_lostKept.title: Lost the Seat, Kept the Man
epilogue: You go back to the classroom on Monday. JSS 2 asks if you are a politician now. "Not today," you say, and teach them the Constitution.

epilogue.text: The video of you shaking the winner's hand goes round the ward. In four years, people say, it might go round again.

p_witness.title: The Witness
epilogue: Baba Oko's Prado is parked at the EFCC office for three weeks. Then it isn't. Nobody knows where it went.
You take the oath of office with your hand on the Constitution and Ifeoma's tape in your pocket.

p_certificate.title: The Certificate
epilogue: The certificate of return is framed in your parlour. Funke has turned it to face the wall twice. You turn it back.
Every time Wahala FM says "investigation", your stomach does something you have to pretend is indigestion.

p_puppet.title: Baba Oko's Boy
epilogue: Wale Oko's company builds the toilets. They are beautiful. They have no water.
You go to Baba Oko's house every Sunday. He calls you "my son". You never correct him.

p_jailed.title: Kirikiri
epilogue: Awaiting trial. The other men in the cell call you "Honourable" and make you settle their quarrels.
Seyi visits once, with Agege bread. "Experience," he says. He doesn't laugh.

p_fled.title: Medical Tourism
epilogue: London is cold and expensive and nobody knows your name, which was the point.
Funke does not come. She sends a voice note: "When you are well, come home. If you are never well, stay."

sugar_saidNo.title: The Woman Who Said No
epilogue: Officer Grace's commendation hangs behind the bar, next to the price list.
Twelve girls who were going to Tripoli are in school, in salons, at home. Some of them send you a message on your birthday.

epilogue.text: The rules on the bar wall: still there, in Kemi's handwriting. Somebody laminated them.
The boy you put in a taxi home: he passed his WAEC. His mother found out where he had been that night. She brought you a cake. You didn't ask how she knew.
The schoolboy you let into the bar: his mother came to the gate a week later. You remember her face better than his.
Kemi's mother: her blood pressure is down. She sends agege bread every month, addressed to "the good madam".
Iya Ajo: back on South Street, collecting again, under supervision. Rukky and you take turns watching her.
Mrs. Adéwálé, the proprietress: she invites you to speak at the school's Career Day. You speak about catering. Everybody knows. Nobody says.
Precious: Microsoft Excel, distinction. She does the books for three shops on South Street now and still laughs too loud.
Jide's borrowed suit jacket still hangs on the bar. It has become a kind of flag.
The crusade: South Street still calls it "the day Mama Sugar turned a crusade into an owambe".
Italy: Precious never went. She keeps Officer Grace's photos in a drawer, for the next girl who asks.
Tari went home to Edo with ₦50,000 and a phone. She calls on the first of every month.
The Wahala FM interview: Ifeoma played it three times. Your real name is out now. It turns out to be lighter to carry than Mama Sugar.
Commander Bassey: still collects on South Street. Never at your gate.

sugar_kitchen.title: Sugar's Kitchen
epilogue: Sugar's Kitchen & Suites. Rooms by the night. Pepper soup by the bowl. Receipts for everything, which Chief Dapo finds very confusing.
Ivie puts it on Instagram. Somebody from Lekki drives two hours for your pepper soup and leaves a tip bigger than the bill.

epilogue: Your stall at the market has four chairs and a queue.
Ivie's school sends a letter: she has been made a prefect. You read it nine times, at the stall, out loud, to customers who did not ask.

sugar_manager.title: Golden Fleece II
epilogue: The hotel is busier than ever. Rukky is very pleased with you.
Some nights you walk past the gate and read the sign out of habit. Then you remember.

sugar_queen.title: Queen of South Street
epilogue: Sugar Palace is the biggest hotel on South Street.
The girls come and go. Not many of them stay long enough for you to learn their real names.

sugar_italy.title: The Price of Italy
epilogue: The trial takes two years. Half a million naira of lawyers.
Blessing's mother comes to court every day, sits in the back row, and never looks at you once.

sugar_lockedOut.title: Locked Out
epilogue: Chief Dapo's padlock is very shiny. You sit on the kerb opposite with your one bag, twenty-two years after Warri, and watch your name come down off the gate.

grace_quarry.title: The Quarry Man
epilogue: You let the Lagos bus go and went back to the quarry. Every stone is a naira. It will take years. You start anyway.

epilogue.text: Nne brings your lunch at noon, the way she brought it to Papa. She sings on the way. The quarry men tease you. You let them.
Chinwe stops counting the year. "You came back early," she says. "That counts double."

epilogue: You keep Papa Ngwo's tortoise stick by the door. The tortoise in his stories always broke his shell in the end. Yours is still whole.
grace_quarry.hint: Some roads out of Lagos are short.

grace_usher.title: The Usher
epilogue: White gloves. A soft voice. People trust your face, so you bring them to the white chair and hold the door.
Kalu becomes an usher too. He is better at it than you. He never laughs. Neither do you.

epilogue.text: Nne still calls on Sundays. She can't say your name. She says "my son" instead, and you hold the phone away from your face until she has finished.

epilogue: Somewhere in the white book there is a page with your father's name on it, and the word NO. You have never looked for it.
grace_usher.hint: A second price is still a price.

grace_lagos.title: Lagos Has You
epilogue: You stayed in Lagos. Lagos keeps you very busy. That is its kindness.

epilogue.text: Bíọ́dún drove to Onitsha without you and brought back a bag of ugu for "the coward who didn't go home". He means it kindly. Mostly.
The money still arrives under your mat. You don't count it. You don't need to. It counts you.

epilogue: Every year, the festival video arrives on WhatsApp. Every year, you watch it twice.
grace_lagos.hint: Home is a road. You have to take it.

u_youthLeader.title: Youth Leader
epilogue: You left Royal Crest for the Honourable's Youth Wing. The car is small. Your face is on the back of it, under his.

epilogue.text: Mama tells the bus stop her son works "in government". She stops saying it after the third Youth Wing rally ends in a fight.

epilogue: Every year the Honourable promises you something bigger. Every year he forgets. You learn to remind him, very visibly.

u_akaraEmpire.title: Akara Empire
epilogue: MAMA SOMTO'S: AKARA FOR SCHOLARS. Three shops, a supermarket deal, and a frozen line in Lekki, where you used to pretend you lived.

epilogue.text: The old corner, saved by a court order, is still the first shop. Mama refuses to move to the nicer one. "The drivers know where I am."
Tamara designs your packaging. She charges you full price. You pay it.

epilogue: Dr. Adébáyọ̀ uses your shops as a case study. Students come to interview Mama. She charges them for the akara.
u_akaraEmpire.hint: Sometimes the business is the degree.

p_steppedDown.title: Party Unity
epilogue: You stepped down for Chief Lanre "in the interest of party unity". The Supervisor for Education job arrived eight months late.
The official car has no battery. Your driver pushes it to the office every morning. The JSS 2 students you used to teach wave at you from the bus stop.

epilogue.text: Funke forgives you on the condition that you never say "party unity" in her house again.

p_classroom.title: The Classroom
epilogue: You went back to JSS 2 and wiped the crown off the blackboard.
Owó Ńlá keeps the seat. The market keeps the padlock. Your students keep asking why.
Twenty years later, one of them, a girl from the market, runs for councillor. She wins clean. She tells the newspapers who taught her civics.

p_deputy.title: The Deputy
epilogue: Deputy Leader of the council. An office, a car, a budget line. The nephew signs everything; you countersign it.
Mama Titi doesn't greet you at the market any more. The toilet key is in the nephew's drawer.

epilogue.text: Seyi tells you, once, drunk: "They were losing, Teacher. You had them. You blinked." He never says it again.

sugar_bornAgain.title: Born Again
epilogue: You closed Sugar Palace on a Wednesday and walked into Redeemed Light with your whole past behind you.
The catering business does weddings, burials and church harvests. Your pepper soup converts more people than Pastor Femi's sermons. He says so himself, on the microphone.

epilogue.text: The girls you looked after come to the harvest. Some of them sit in the front row. Mrs. Dapo moves up to make room.
Ivie sings in the youth choir. Better than you. She says so herself, also on the microphone.

sugar_warri.title: Back to Warri
epilogue: Warri. Your mother's compound, a stall for starch and banga, and a daughter who sleeps through the night for the first time in years.

epilogue.text: Kokoro runs Sugar Palace as a real hotel now. Receipts. Locks on the inside. He sends you a photo of every customer complaint, so you can laugh.
Sugar Palace is somebody else's now. Kokoro still sleeps at the gate. Old habits.

epilogue: Sometimes, at night, you can still hear a generator in your head. It is quieter every month.

back_home_early.title: Back to Ìlú-Àlàáfíà
epilogue: You went home on the night bus with Mama asleep on your shoulder. The debt came with you: ₦{debt}, and Iya Bọ́sẹ̀'s patience.
You farm Papa's old plot and carry cement on market days, like he did. It pays slowly. It pays.

epilogue.text: Ada sends fabric on the Ìlú-Àlàáfíà bus every Christmas, with a note: "For Mama. Not for you."
Mama tells the village her son was an agbero in Lagos. She says it proudly, the way you say somebody survived a war.

back_home_early.hint: The first raid isn't the end of the road.

danfo_life.title: No Condition Is Permanent
epilogue: You drive the Oshodi route in a yellow danfo with one wiper. You pay fees at every stop, with exact change.

epilogue.text: Bíọ́dún drives the bus behind you every morning, hooting "God's Time Is The Best!" at every agbero you used to know.

epilogue: Some nights you park under the bridge and listen to Wahala FM report on who became chairman of the park. It isn't you. It doesn't need to be.

the_teacher.title: The New Professor
epilogue: Every morning at five, on crates around an old chair at the Back Side, you teach the rules to whoever came on the night bus.

epilogue.text: Giggles comes once, stands at the back, and doesn't laugh. The next week he brings two boys from Under-Bridge.
Professor comes to listen sometimes. He corrects your Rule 19. You let him.

epilogue: Rule 53, in your handwriting: "Nobody gives you a receipt for nothing. So give one."
the_teacher.hint: Somebody has to teach the next JJC.
